title-group.article-title: Organ-metastatic landscape delineates overall and site-specific immune-related adverse events of PD-L1 blockade in advanced NSCLC

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: It remains unknown whether metastases to different organs confer varying susceptibility to immune-related adverse events (irAEs) within a specific tumor type. We conducted a retrospective study included 708 advanced patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who received atezolizumab in two randomized controlled trials (OAK and POPLAR). Overall, irAEs were less frequent in patients with bone (OR = 0.52, p = 0.039) and pleural effusion metastases (OR = 0.65, p = 0.039), while more frequent in those with brain metastasis (OR = 1.96, p = 0.023). Cumulative irAEs risk differed significantly for patients with extra-thoracic (p = 0.034) but not intra-thoracic metastases (p = 0.680). In terms of site-specific irAEs, hepatitis, hypothyroidism, and rash were less frequent in patients with bone metastasis, whereas pneumonitis, adrenal insufficiency, and ocular inflammatory toxicity were more concentrated in patients with brain metastasis. A metastasis-based scoring system was developed by integrating the organ-metastatic landscape to identify high-risk populations for irAEs among NSCLC patients received PD-L1 blockade (p = 0.009). These findings highlight the predictive value of the organ-metastatic landscape for irAEs in advanced NSCLC received PD-L1 blockade.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The emergence of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) that block programmed death-(ligand) 1 (PD-[L]1) and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte–associated antigen 4 (CTLA-4) has gradually become a cornerstone therapy for advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)1–3. Despite the durable antitumor response, ICIs use is associated with a spectrum of immune-related adverse events (irAEs), which are major challenges in the clinical application4–6. IrAEs can occur in virtually all organs and encompass more than 70 distinct pathologies, including hepatitis, colitis, pneumonia, arthritis, and myocarditis7,8. Immunotherapy may be suspended for toxicities and corticosteroids may be administered, which can compromise anti-tumor immunity9,10. Therefore, identifying patients at high risk for irAEs is crucial for optimizing immunotherapy strategies.

It has been reported that the patterns of irAEs during immunotherapy vary among tumors of different origins11. Given that patients with advanced cancer frequently present with multiple metastases, whether metastases in different organs confer varying susceptibility to overall or site-specific irAEs in a specific primary tumor type remains unknown. Besides, our previous research found that metastatic landscape is associated with the efficacy of immunotherapy in patients with NSCLC12. Given the coupling nature of efficacy and toxicity of immunotherapy, we hypothesize that the baseline organ-metastatic landscape may also influence irAE patterns following PD-L1 blockade in advanced NSCLC. Unlike the primary tumor at the early stage, research focused on a single tumor lesion has limited clinical significance in the late stage of NSCLC, as tumors may spread to multiple organs simultaneously in the advanced or metastatic setting. Therefore, a comprehensive understanding of the impact of organ metastases on irAEs necessitates integrating various metastatic sites. For this purpose, a metastasis-based scoring system for irAEs was developed to comprehensively evaluate the impact of organ metastases on the risk of irAEs.

sec.title: Differences in incidence and onset of overall irAEs according to baseline metastatic landscape
sec.p: Clinical characteristics of the patients in OAK and POPLAR cohorts were generally similar between the two study groups (Supplementary Table 1). Of the 708 patients treated with immunotherapy, 440 (62.1%) were male and 268 (37.9%) were female, and the mean age was 62.4 years (SD, 9.8 years). The numbers of patients with rash, hepatitis, and hypothyroidism were 147 (24.5%), 88 (53.7%), and 47 (21.8%), respectively (Fig. 1A). A total of 643 patients (90.8%) had intrapulmonary metastasis (Fig. 1B). In this study, 260 (36.7%) patients developed at least one kind of irAEs and the median time to onset of irAEs was 106 days (IQR, 27-332 days). As for site-specific irAEs, immune-related rash and hepatitis occurred earlier, whereas hypothyroidism occurred at a later phase (Supplementary Fig. 1). The incidence of overall irAEs was highest in patients with brain metastasis (27 of 55, 49.1%) while patients with bone metastasis had the lowest incidence of overall irAEs (57 of 219, 26.0%) (Fig. 1C). Besides, patients with bone metastasis had less co-occurrence rate of different site-specific irAEs, while patients with brain and adrenal metastases had higher rates (Supplementary Fig. 2).

caption.title: Landscape of metastases and irAEs in patients with advanced NSCLC treated with atezolizumab.
caption.p: A Percentages of various types of irAEs. B Percentages of each type of organ metastasis. C Percentages of incidence of irAEs in patients with different organ metastases. The number within parentheses is the real number of cases. D Multivariate logistic regression analysis and multivariate cox regression analysis for the risk of irAEs based on organ metastases. MET metastasis, OR odd ratio, HR hazard ratio, PEFF pleural effusion, MEDIA mediastinum.

sec.p: To investigate the impact of baseline organ metastases on overall irAEs, we conducted multivariate logistic regression analysis and cox regression analysis to explore the incidence and onset of overall irAEs, respectively. Remarkably, different organ metastases at baseline yielded significantly different incidence of overall irAEs during anti-PD-L1 treatment (Fig. 1D). Among them, bone metastasis (OR, 0.52 [95% CI, 0.34–0.69]; p < 0.001) and malignant pleural effusion (OR, 0.65 [95% CI, 0.42–0.97]; p = 0.01) were significant protective factors for overall irAEs. As for the timing of irAE occurrence, patients with bone metastasis showed significantly later onset of irAEs (HR, 0.66 [95% CI, 0.48–0.89]; p = 0.007). Furthermore, multivariate analysis identified brain metastasis as the only independent factor associated with an increased risk of overall irAEs (OR, 1.96 [95% CI, 1.09–3.54]; p = 0.02).

Pairwise comparisons among patients with different organ metastases showed that bone metastasis and malignant pleural effusion yielded less occurrence of overall irAEs compared with metastases to other organs, especially brain and adrenal gland metastases (Fig. 2A). Specifically, patients with brain metastasis had the highest risk among all the metastatic groups, which was significantly higher than that in patients with bone metastasis (OR, 2.74 [95% CI, 1.49–5.05]; p = 0.001). A consistent observation was shown in terms of the timing of irAE occurrence, where the most significant difference of irAE onset was shown between brain metastasis and bone metastasis (HR, 1.84 [95% CI, 1.16–2.90]; p = 0.010) (Fig. 2B). Given the pronounced difference in terms of irAEs among metastases to bone, brain, and adrenal glands, instead of those metastases to mediastinum and pleura, we asked whether extrathoracic metastases played more important role than intrathoracic metastases on irAEs. Interestingly, the cumulative risk was significantly different among extrapulmonary metastases (Fig. 2C), whereas no difference was observed among intrapulmonary metastases, according to the onset of irAEs (Fig. 2D). Furthermore, we analyzed some other clinical outcomes related to irAEs. Patients with brain metastasis showed a lower proportion of recovery from irAEs; however, this difference did not reach statistical significance (Supplementary Fig. 3). In addition, no statistically significant associations were observed between metastatic organ sites and irAE grade or treatment discontinuation due to irAEs (Supplementary Tables 2–3).

caption.title: Pairwise comparison of overall irAEs based on organ metastatic status.
caption.p: Pairwise comparisons of OR (A) and HR (B) among patients with row-defining organ metastases versus column-defining organ metastases. Significant results are in red font. Kaplan-Meier curves comparing cumulative hazard per metastatic organs among intrathoracic metastatic organs (C) and extrathoracic metastatic organs (D). MEDIA mediastinum, MET metastasis, PEFF pleural effusion, ADREN adrenal gland.

sec.title: Association between baseline metastatic landscape and site-specific irAEs
sec.p: Given the association between overall irAEs and the baseline organ metastasis landscape, particularly extrathoracic metastases, we further investigated the relationship between various extrathoracic metastases and site-specific irAEs (Fig. 3A, B). Multivariate analyses revealed that hepatitis (OR, 0.55 [95% CI, 0.32–0.95]; p = 0.03), hypothyroidism (OR, 0.27 [95% CI, 0.11–0.71]; p = 0.008), and rash (OR, 0.63 [95% CI, 0.41–0.95]; p = 0.04) were less frequent in patients with bone metastasis, whereas pneumonia (OR, 3.25 [95% CI, 1.02–10.30]; p = 0.05), adrenal insufficiency (OR, 12.71 [95% CI, 1.52–106.20]; p = 0.02) and ocular inflammatory toxicity (OR, 21.17 [95% CI, 1.73–258.29]; p = 0.02) were more concentrated in patients with brain metastasis. As for the onset timing of site-specific irAEs, patients with bone metastasis experienced significantly later hypothyroidism (HR, 0.36 [95% CI, 0.14–0.91]; p = 0.03), while those with metastases to brain (HR, 7.81 [95% CI, 1.09–55.82]; p = 0.04) and adrenal glands (HR, 12.54 [95% CI, 1.30–120.78]; p = 0.03) developed earlier adrenal insufficiency. Of note, there is a significant difference of the onset of pneumonitis, one of the most frequent and severe irAEs, among patients with different extrathoracic metastases (Fig. 3C).

caption.title: The pattern of site-specific irAEs per baseline organ metastases.
caption.p: Multivariate logistic regression analysis (A) and multivariate cox regression analysis (B) for the risk of site-specific irAEs in patients with extrathoracic metastases. C Kaplan-Meier analyses of pneumonitis in patients with extrathoracic metastases. Kaplan-Meier analyses of adrenal insufficiency in patients with or without adrenal gland metastasis (D) and hepatitis in patients with or without liver metastasis (E). MET metastasis, OR odds ratio, HR hazard ratio, ADREN adrenal gland.

sec.p: Interestingly, liver metastasis (Fig. 3D) and adrenal metastasis (Fig. 3E) exerted greater susceptibility to irAEs in the metastatic lesions themselves. Adrenal insufficiency was more common (OR, 15.22 [95% CI, 1.45–159.59]; p = 0.02) and occurred earlier (HR, 12.54 [95% CI, 1.30–120.78]; p = 0.03) in patients with adrenal gland metastasis compared to those without adrenal gland metastasis, while hepatitis occurred earlier in patients with liver metastasis (HR, 1.81 [95% CI, 1.11–2.94]; p = 0.02), with a trend towards higher incidence (OR, 1.56 [95% CI, 0.91–2.65]; p = 0.10) compared to those without liver metastasis. In addition, patients with liver metastasis also develop colitis earlier (HR, 5.49 [95% CI, 1.14–26.36]; p = 0.03) and rash later (HR, 0.57 [95% CI, 0.34–0.95]; p = 0.03).

sec.title: Metastasis-based model forecasting high-risk population of irAEs
sec.p: Based on the above results, three metastatic types (brain, adrenal gland, and pleura metastases) were identified to exhibit a positive correlation trend with irAEs. We found that when the number of these irAE-associated metastases was greater than or equal to two, the risk of developing irAEs increased significantly (Supplementary Fig. 4). The synergistic value of different metastatic organs inspired us to incorporate the whole landscape for comprehensive assessment, accounting for the contributions of both protective organs (e.g., bone) and irAE-associated organs (e.g., brain). Therefore, we proposed a scoring system named METscore-irAEs to forecast cumulative hazard of advanced NSCLC patients treated with anti-PD-L1 therapy by integrating the baseline extrathoracic metastatic landscape (Fig. 4A). According to the METscore-irAEs system, an irAE risk score was estimated for each patient in the pooled OAK and POPLAR cohort, and patients were divided into two groups according to the Maximally Selected Rank Statistics (MSRS)13. Notably, we observed a general pattern of higher risk and earlier onset of irAEs relative to those with higher risk score (p = 0.009) (Fig. 4B).

caption.title: Metastasis-based scoring system incorporating metastatic landscape for prediction of irAEs.
caption.p: A Nomogram illustrating scaled points as proxy for each metastatic organ. B METscore-irAEs forecasts cumulative hazard of irAEs. Kaplan-Meier curves showing cumulative hazard according to METscore-irAEs groups. Patients were stratified into high and low risk groups according to the Maximally Selected Rank Statistics. irAE immune-related adverse event, MET metastasis.

sec.p: To gain a more comprehensive understanding of the risk factors for irAEs, we performed univariate analyses on clinical indicators and identified associations between the occurrence and onset of irAEs with ANA, neutrophil percentage, as well as EGFR mutation and ALK rearrangements (Supplementary Fig. 5). These clinical indicators, along with the METscore-irAE model, were then included in multivariate logistic and Cox regression analyses, where the METscore-irAE derived risk groups remained an independent predictor for both the incidence and the time to onset of irAEs (Supplementary Table 4). To verify whether the model is applicable to other cohorts, we included patients receiving immunotherapy from the BIRCH and IMpower110 studies as a validation cohort (Supplementary Table 5). Similarly, patients were stratified into high- and low-risk groups based on MSRS, and the high-risk group yielded a significantly higher incidence of irAEs compared with the low-risk group (Supplementary Fig. 6). Univariate and Multivariate logistic regression demonstrated that METscore-irAEs independently predicted irAEs in the validation cohort (Supplementary Table 6).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In several clinical trials involved atezolizumab, 45–60% of NSCLC patients experienced irAEs14–16. Although the understanding of the mechanism of irAE is constantly fulfilling, preventative strategies has not yet routinely applied in clinical practice17. In this study, we observed a differential predictive value for overall and site-specific irAEs among various baseline organ metastases. We delineated and integrated the predictive effects of metastatic-organ landscape to forecast irAEs of advanced NSCLC patients receiving anti-PD-L1 therapy.

To our knowledge, this is the first study to explore the relationship between irAEs and tumor metastases. We presume that the tumor microenvironment, adaptive immune responses, and neoantigen formation may be shaped by organ-specific immunity18–20, potentially explaining the variation in irAE profiles across different metastatic sites. Although bone metastasis seems to curb the occurrence of irAEs, this benefit may come at the cost of reduced efficacy of immunotherapy. Previous studies indicated limited clinical benefits of immunotherapy for patients with bone metastasis12,21. Specifically, bone marrow, rich in various immune cells, can function as a site of primary or memory immune response and plays a crucial role in regulating systemic immunity22. Bone metastasis may cause bone marrow damage, leading to suppressed hematopoiesis and impaired immune function. In contrast, brain metastasis is a risk factor of irAEs. The unique features of the brain contribute to its traditionally immune-privileged status, including the presence of the blood-brain barrier, specialized environmental cells (microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and neurons), and the composition of the extracellular matrix23,24. The invasion of tumor cells may partially disrupt the blood-brain barrier and alter the function of resident cells and the extracellular matrix, compromising immune privilege and potentially facilitating irAEs25.

Building on these observations, it is important to consider how organ-specific metastatic sites may influence the balance between efficacy and toxicity of immunotherapy. Previous studies have suggested that the efficacy and toxicity of immunotherapy are generally coupled26,27, which is consistent with our findings in patients with brain and bone metastases. As for liver metastasis, it tended to confer a protective effect against irAEs although without reaching significant level. Interestingly, liver metastasis has been characterized as a well-established negative prognostic factor, and patients with liver metastasis generally experience poorer outcomes when treated with immunotherapy as a single agent12,28. Together, these observations underscore the importance of considering immune-related toxicity when evaluating therapeutic benefit in metastatic NSCLC treated with ICIs.

The timing of irAE onset is variable among different organs. Most irAEs have a median time to onset within 38 weeks of initiating ICI therapy, with skin toxicities, myocarditis, colitis, hepatitis, acute kidney injury, and thyroid dysfunction tending to occur relatively early, typically with median onset times ranging from 4 to 14 weeks1,8,29–32. In contrast, pneumonitis and rheumatologic irAEs generally manifest later, with median onset times between 34 and 38 weeks1. In addition, we found that some site-specific irAEs seem to be more likely to occur at the site of metastatic injury. Immune-related toxicity may arise when T cells recognize antigens shared between tumor cells and normal tissues33. A previous study identified T-cell antigens that are common to tumor tissues and normal tissues in some specific organs, providing a potential explanation for the variation in incidence of organ-specific irAEs34. The “seed and soil” hypothesis suggested that, when a plant goes to seed, its seeds are carried in all directions but can only live and grow if they fall on congenial soil; tumor cells that colonize other tissues can adapt to the local microenvironment, acquiring features more similar to the surrounding normal cells35,36. This similarity—potentially in antigen presentation and surface markers—between metastatic lesions and adjacent normal tissues may contribute to the tendency for irAEs to occur in the metastatic organs.

Currently, many studies found the association between autoimmunity and some potential blood-based biomarkers37–39. Although no consensus has been reached, substantial evidence suggests that baseline levels of absolute neutrophil, lymphocyte, monocyte, eosinophil, and basophil counts, along with their increases during follow-up, are associated with a higher risk of irAEs40–42. A systematic review and meta-analysis encompassing 25 studies indicated that a high neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio is an independent risk factor for irAE occurrence41. In addition to laboratory biomarkers, the immune-oncology field has also evaluated clinical features that confer heightened risk of irAEs43,44. Compared to clinical features, obtaining laboratory biomarker information not only faces higher costs and technical requirements, but patients sometimes also need to undergo invasive examinations. The metastasis-based model only requires imaging detection, which is a necessary examination for clinical treatment at present, without additional costs or harm to patients. As tumor metastasis is a common clinical phenomenon, the METscore-irAEs model might provide practical reference support for frontline clinical doctors in the management of irAEs during ICI therapy.

Our study had several limitations. First, the present study is a post-hoc study with unavoidable confounding factors. A larger scale prospective study should be conducted in the future. Second, due to sample size limitation, there was insufficient statistical power to perform subgroup analyses based on different PD-L1 expression levels and irAE grades. Since the patients from OAK and POPLAR studies had received prior first-line chemotherapy, the applicability of our findings to patients receiving first-line immunotherapy remains further exploration. Besides, the absence of data on patients’ pre-existing underlying diseases, a potential confounding factor, may have led to an overestimation of the association between organ-specific irAEs and metastases. Moreover, this is a study on advanced NSCLC patients using atezolizumab, and further confirmation is needed to determine whether this phenomenon still exists for other ICI types and cancers.

In conclusion, our study suggest that the presence of different organ metastases could exert different impart on the incidence and onset of overall and site-specific irAEs. The baseline organ-metastatic landscape might be a predictive factor for overall and site-specific irAEs in advanced NSCLC patients received PD-L1 blockade. Our findings enhance the understanding of organ-specific immunity in immunotherapy under the metastatic setting of NSCLC and may inform personalized immunotherapy strategies for irAEs.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: All patients enrolled provided signed informed consent in accordance with the protocols of the corresponding studies. Deidentified individual-participant data of these clinical trials were accessed according to Roche’s policy and process for clinical study data sharing. We pooled the OAK and POPLAR cohorts for analyses as their similarities in study design. Information on baseline organ metastases, as well as the incidence and onset of various irAEs were collected. Overall irAEs refer to the collection of any site-specific irAE; the occurrence of any site-specific irAE is considered as the occurrence of overall irAEs. We explored the association between baseline metastases with overall irAEs and pairwise comparisons among patients with different organ metastases were performed. Moreover, analysis of association between site-specific irAEs and metastatic landscape was conducted. Finally, a metastasis-based scoring system (METscore-irAEs) was then set up to incorporate each metastatic organ by calculating the total points in forecasting risk of overall irAEs (Fig. 5). Patients treated with immunotherapy from the BIRCH and IMpower110 trials were used for validation. In this study, the irAE incidence was defined as the primary endpoint represented by odds ratio (OR), and the time to irAEs was the co-primary endpoint represented by hazard ratio (HR).

sec.title: Population
sec.p: We conducted a post-hoc analysis of individual-participant data from two randomized controlled trials (OAK: NCT02008227; POPLAR: NCT01903993)45,46, providing a total sample size of 1403 advanced NSCLC patients. OAK and POPLAR were randomized phase III and II trials, respectively, comparing atezolizumab versus docetaxel in previously treated NSCLC patients45,46. Treatment started at the time of randomization and was administered until unacceptable toxicity or disease progression. For the current study, a subset of 708 patients who received atezolizumab was included: 575 from OAK and 133 from POPLAR. Detailed information of these two cohorts have been described in the corresponding studies45,46. Additionally, two trials (BIRCH: NCT02031458; IMpower110: NCT02409342) were pooled as validation cohort47,48. The BIRCH trial enrolled patients with advanced NSCLC treated with atezolizumab, who had previously received 0–2 or more lines of chemotherapy. Patients whose tumor cells (TC) or tumor-infiltrating immune cells (IC) expressed PD-L1 ≥ 5% were included in this trial47. IMpower110 was a randomized, open-label, phase 3 trial involving patients with metastatic non-squamous or squamous NSCLC who had not received prior chemotherapy48. A subset of 516 patients was included in the present study due to the data availability: 358 from BIRCH and 158 from IMpower110.

sec.title: Metastatic landscape and irAEs
sec.p: The metastatic-organ landscape comprised adrenal glands, brain, bone, lung, liver, pleura, pleural effusion, mediastinum, and others (metastases to abdominal wall, abdominal cavity, marrow, chest, skin, and other unknown sites, each with a frequency <2%) in the present study. The irAEs involved in this study are adrenal insufficiency, colitis, diabetes mellitus, encephalitis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, hemolytic anemia, hepatitis, hyperthyroidism, hypophysitis, hypothyroidism, meningitis, meningoencephalitis, myocarditis, myositis, nephritis, ocular inflammatory toxicity, pancreatitis, pneumonitis, rash, severe cutaneous reaction, and vasculitis.

sec.title: Development of a metastasis-based scoring system for irAE prediction
sec.p: We first performed multiple logistic regression analysis to establish a predictive model for the incidence rate of overall irAEs using OAK and POPLAR data. The model coefficients are scaled from –10 to 10 and rounded to the nearest integer for clinical use. The scaled points corresponding to the metastatic statuses of organs delineated overall irAE risk. Then, by calculating the total score, a METscore-irAEs was established to predict the incidence of overall irAEs, incorporating the effect of each metastatic organ. Patients were divided into two groups according to the cut-point based on Maximally Selected Rank Statistics (MSRS)13, and Kaplan-Meier analysis was performed to test the predictive value for irAEs.

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: The association between the baseline metastatic status and both overall and site-specific irAEs was analyzed using logistic regression and Cox regression, expressed as OR and HR, respectively, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The Kaplan-Meier method with the log-rank test was leveraged to compare the cumulative risk of irAEs based on organ-specific metastatic status. Time to irAEs was defined as the interval between a patient’s randomization into the clinical study and the first occurrence of the irAEs or the time of study discontinuation. Kaplan-Meier analyses were conducted in R (version 4.3.1) with R packages “survival” and “survminer”. Multivariate Cox proportional hazard regression was implemented using R package “survival”. All statistical tests were two sided, and p < 0.05 was deemed statistically significant.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: The data associated with the study has been deposited into a global clinical research data sharing platform called Vivli (https://vivli.org/, Data Request ID: 10158, 11201). The authors do not have permission to share data. Requests to access the datasets could be made directly to the platform via their data access request forms.
